title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-breadcrumbs
content:
Context / summary:
- Intermittent failures observed when clients consume long-running server-sent events (text/event-stream) from the runtime. Failures manifest as truncated streams, occasional 504s from ingress proxy, and client-side EPIPE/connection reset errors under load. Seems correlated with backpressure from slow consumer + intermediate proxies (nginx/envoy/haproxy).

What I've seen / breadcrumbs:
- Local dev (no proxy) + curl -N: stream is fine for large sessions (~30m).
- Through staging ingress (nginx + envoy) reproducible: after ~10–30s of slow consumption, the client sees truncated response and server logs show "upstream prematurely closed connection" or "write EPIPE".
- Reproduced with a very simple server that flushes chunks every 200ms. Works locally, breaks when routed via ingress.
- Symptoms vary: sometimes 504 from proxy (timeout while buffering), sometimes immediate connection reset.

Error snippets from logs (staging):
- "upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream"
- "upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out)"
- "write EPIPE"
- client: "curl: (18) transfer closed with outstanding read data remaining"
- "stream truncated: expected final chunk; got EOF" (from client-side sanity check)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Proxy/nginx buffering and timeouts: nginx by default buffers responses and can wait for full response; with slow-consuming clients this can hit buffers/timeouts.
2) Gzip/compression + buffering causing proxy to wait for larger buffers before flushing down to client.
3) TCP-level Nagle/coalescing + proxy TCP timeouts interacting with our flush frequency.
4) Connection pooling/idle timeouts at load balancer (ALB/Envoy) closing upstream prematurely when downstream is slow.
5) Runtime not actually flushing after write (we think it is, but a library change might have reintroduced buffering).

Commands / repro steps I used:
- Minimal curl stream (raw SSE consumption):
  curl -v -N \
    -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
    "https://staging-api.redwood.internal/v1/generate/stream?model=test-small"

- Observed output: initial event(s) then after ~15s the transfer closes with curl: (18)

- Raw netcat test (simulate slow client):
  # server side: (node) write chunks every 200ms and flush
  printf 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/event-stream\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\n\r\n' | nc -l 8081
  # client side slow reader: read 1 byte, sleep 0.5s
  pv -L 2k < <(curl -s "http://localhost:8081/stream")

- wrk load to simulate many concurrent clients:
  wrk -t4 -c200 -d30s -s ./sse-wrk.lua http://staging-ingress/load-test
  (lua script reads chunked SSE response but sleeps between reads to simulate backpressure)

- Node fetch-based client to reproduce backpressure (example):
  const res = await fetch(url, { headers: { Accept: 'text/event-stream' } });
  const reader = res.body.getReader();
  while(true) {
    const { value, done } = await reader.read();
    if (done) break;
    // artificially slow processing
    await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 150));
  }

- Verified behavior differs if we remove proxies: direct to runtime host + same slow client = no truncation in most runs.

Things tried and their results:
- nginx config: set proxy_buffering off; proxy_request_buffering off; sendfile off; tcp_nodelay on -> reduced frequency of truncation but not eliminated.
- Disabled gzip at proxy and runtime -> helped in some runs (less buffering), still not perfect.
- Increased proxy timeouts (proxy_read_timeout) -> fewer 504s but still occasional truncation.
- Adjusted runtime to increase explicit flush frequency (flush after every chunk) -> better, but still fails under high concurrency.
- Switched to HTTP/1.1 keepalive disabled -> no meaningful change.
- Replaced nginx with Envoy in staging -> similar failures, points to LB/timeouts or client-side flow.
- Added application-level sequence numbers + final event marker to detect truncation -> useful for detecting which chunk missing.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Are there any intermediate LBs (cloud LB/ALB) that might have hard limits for idle per-connection time? Need to check cloud infra config for staging.
- Can we get tcpdump between proxy <-> runtime during a reproduce? Need coordination with infra.
- Are there any recent changes to our runtime http server lib (e.g., switching from netty X to Y) that could affect flush semantics?

Immediate next steps I plan to try:
- Obtain tcpdump (proxy <-> runtime) during a controlled repro to see whether runtime is still sending chunks and whether proxy is ACKing.
- Create a minimal end-to-end repro that runs in staging (simple runtime container that emits numbered chunks every 200ms) and a dedicated client that reads slowly. Start with 1 client, then scale to many. Capture pcap + logs.
- Add additional logging in runtime around write/flush calls (timestamps, bytes written, syscall errors) to confirm whether EPIPE originates from write or upstream close.
- Try worst-case: reduce chunk interval to 50ms and see whether more frequent flush eliminates buffering issues (if related to proxy heuristics).
- Reach out to infra to check LB idle timeouts and any connection management (AWS ALB has idle timeout default 60s).

Quick repro I can run locally (node):
- server.js (quick):
  const http = require('http');
  http.createServer((req, res) => {
    res.writeHead(200, {
      "Content-Type": "text/event-stream",
      "Cache-Control": "no-cache",
      "Connection": "keep-alive"
    });
    let i = 0;
    const t = setInterval(() => {
      i++;
      const chunk = `data: {\"seq\":${i}, \"ts\":${Date.now()} }\\n\\n`;
      res.write(chunk);
      // some frameworks need explicit flush, Node streams flush on write
      if (i > 1000) { clearInterval(t); res.end(); }
    }, 200);
  }).listen(8080);

- client (slow reader):
  curl -v -N http://localhost:8080/ | pv -qL 1k (or the Node reader above)

If you want to reproduce on staging: replace host with https://staging-api.redwood.internal/v1/generate/stream and add auth header.

Notes for infra/ops:
- If possible, enable tcp_keepalive probes and increase LB idle timeout to 5 minutes for streaming routes.
- For nginx: proxy_buffering off + chunked_transfer_encoding on + disable gzip for those routes. For Envoy: set no_host_header, idle_timeout, and downstream_socket_options tcp_nodelay.
- Consider an explicit "heartbeat" event from runtime every X seconds when no data to keep downstream alive.

Conclusion:
- Likely multi-factor: proxy buffering + compression + LB idle/timeout interactions cause upstream to be closed when client is slow. Need pcap + logs to nail root cause. Next: coordinate with infra to capture pcap and run controlled experiments on staging with different proxies (nginx vs envoy) and with increased logging on runtime write path.

Appendix: quick curl + debug flags I ran:
- curl --http1.1 -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" -H "Authorization: Bearer REDWOOD_API_KEY" "https://staging-ingress.redwood/v1/stream?model=test"
- curl -v -N --raw --no-keepalive ...

Recorded test IDs:
- wrk run: run-2024-11-15-1203 (attached in /tmp/wrk-runs)
